entries.clue: Penny, say, returns to mother for cassava (6)

indicatorNotes.say: 'Say' tacked on to a word marks it as one instance of something wider, so what is wanted is the class the penny belongs to.
indicatorNotes.returns: Something that returns comes back the way it went, so the letters are read from the far end first.

blocks.note: ma is the nursery word for mother
a penny is one example of a coin, and COIN turned back reads NIOC

annotation.surface: A woman called Penny going back home to her mother.
annotation.walkthrough: Penny reads as a name and is a coin; 'say' is the small word asking for the class rather than the instance. Manioc and cassava are two names for the same tropical root, one of them by way of Portuguese.
annotation.definitionFit: Manioc is the starchy tropical root crop sold as cassava — the two words name the same plant.

entries.clue: Following the trend, to a certain extent (5,1,7)

annotation.definitionNote: The first definition is the phrase taken literally, with 'after' in its chasing sense, so it describes someone in pursuit of a trend rather than offering a synonym for the idiom.

blocks.note: read as chasing whatever is in vogue, with 'after' in its in-pursuit-of sense
the idiom's worn-down sense: up to a point, and no further

annotation.surface: Somebody keeping up with whatever happens to be in vogue this season.
annotation.walkthrough: 'After' carries two senses at once: in pursuit of something, and the idiom's worn-down 'sort of'. The enumeration gives the second reading away, since very few phrases park a lone A in the middle.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone after a fashion is chasing a trend, while the idiom 'after a fashion' means only partly — doing something to a certain extent.

entries.clue: Repeat there's a point in ragged attire (7)

indicatorNotes.ragged: Something ragged is torn out of its proper shape, so the letters beside it will not stay in the order given.

blocks.note: east is a point of the compass, and E is its letter
anagram fodder, six letters
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: The suggestion that there is something to be said for dressing in shabby clothes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Repeat' at the front looks like an instruction to the solver rather than a definition. A point in a clue is nearly always the compass kind, and E is the one that makes the letters come out.
annotation.definitionFit: To iterate something is to say or do it over again, the plain verb sense of repeat.

entries.clue: We hear emblems represent percussion instruments (7)

indicatorNotes.We hear: What we hear reaches us as noise, so the word beside it is taken by its sound and not by its spelling.

blocks.note: emblems are symbols, and SYMBOLS spoken aloud is spelt the other way

annotation.surface: A claim that a set of badges is standing in for the instruments at the back of the band.
annotation.walkthrough: The sound-alike carries the whole clue, so there are no letters to assemble. 'Represent' looks like wordplay and only points one half of the clue at the other.
annotation.definitionFit: Cymbals are the brass plates clashed together at the back of an orchestra, part of the percussion section.

entries.clue: Flowers untidily spilt around top of urn (6)

indicatorNotes.untidily: Anything done untidily comes out in no proper order, so those letters are not to be left as they stand.
indicatorNotes.around: Around means encircling, so the shuffled letters close in on either side of the one that follows.
indicatorNotes.top of: The top of a word is where it starts, so only its opening letter is taken.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, five letters
the opening letter of URN
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: Blooms tipped over in a mess all around the rim of an urn.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spilt' is both what happened in the picture and the word whose letters move, which is why the clue reads so smoothly. Flowers here is the straight sense, not the setter's other favourite — a river that flows.
annotation.definitionFit: Tulips are the cup-shaped spring blooms grown from bulbs, so they are flowers in the plain sense.

entries.clue: Goes with seabirds, say (5)

indicatorNotes.say: Say can mean utter, so the word before it is judged by the noise it makes when spoken.

blocks.note: terns are the slender fork-tailed seabirds, and TERNS said aloud gives the answer's sound

annotation.surface: Whatever it is that keeps company with the birds out over the water.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Goes' has to be read as a noun: a go at something is a turn at it, which is why the definition is plural. 'Say' is a homophone flag here rather than its usual 'for example'.
annotation.definitionFit: A go at something is a turn at it — three goes on the swing are three turns — so the plural nouns swap cleanly.

entries.clue: Defamation of the Spanish after liberation (5)

indicatorNotes.after: In a down clue 'after' sends what stands before it further down the column, so the article follows rather than leads.

blocks.note: lib is the everyday short form of liberation, as in women's lib
el is Spanish for 'the'

annotation.surface: A slur aimed at Spaniards once they have been set free.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The Spanish' means the Spanish word for 'the' rather than the people — worth spotting early, since French LE and LA and Italian IL work the same way. Defamation in print is libel; spoken, it is slander.
annotation.definitionFit: Libel is defamation in permanent form: a published false statement that damages somebody's reputation.

entries.clue: Authorisation for take-off? (6,7)

blocks.note: read as official permission of any kind, and meant as the particular permission a printed certificate carries
read as a comic impersonation, and meant as the moment an aircraft leaves the ground

annotation.surface: Written permission to do an impression of somebody.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Take-off' is a comic impersonation before it is anything an aeroplane does, and the question mark marks the clue as a joke rather than a dictionary entry. There is no wordplay to find: one definition, read two ways.
annotation.definitionFit: A pilot's licence is the certificate authorising its holder to fly an aircraft, and taking off is the part of flying the joke settles on.

entries.clue: Pennant flown by ship circling river (8)

indicatorNotes.circling: Something circling another thing goes round the outside of it, so the long word closes over the letter named next.

blocks.note: a steamer is a ship driven by steam
r is the map-maker's abbreviation for river

annotation.surface: A flag flying from a boat as it goes round and round on the river.
annotation.walkthrough: The container hides behind a picture in which a ship really could circle — except that no ship circles a river, and that impossibility is the tell. Pennant and the answer are both long tapering flags.
annotation.definitionFit: A streamer is a long narrow flag or ribbon flown from a masthead, which is what a pennant is.

entries.clue: One charging 50 points? (4)

annotation.definitionNote: The second definition is by score rather than by synonym — the thing is not fifty points but what fifty points are awarded for — which is what the question mark concedes.

blocks.note: the beast that lowers its head and runs at whatever annoyed it
the score for the small red circle at the dead centre of a dartboard

annotation.surface: Somebody levying a fee of fifty points.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface wants 'charging' read as billing, and the whole clue as one person's price list. Both halves are definitions: the animal that charges, and the red disc at the centre of a dartboard.
annotation.definitionFit: A bull charges at whatever provokes it, and in darts the bull is the middle of the board, worth fifty.

entries.clue: Caesarean section department (4)

indicatorNotes.section: A section is a piece cut out of something larger, so a run of letters is lifted from the word beside it.

blocks.note: CaesAREAn carries the letters in its middle, already in order

annotation.surface: The hospital unit where Caesareans are carried out.
annotation.walkthrough: A Caesarean section is a real surgical term, so the two words look welded together and neither seems to be doing crossword work. The definition is 'department' in the sense of 'that's not my department'.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody's area is their department — the patch of responsibility they own, as in 'sales is her area'.

entries.clue: Unqualified sailor thus has instrument (8)

blocks.note: an AB is an able seaman, the rating above ordinary seaman
so means thus — it follows, therefore
a lute is the pear-bodied plucked string instrument

annotation.surface: A sailor with no certificates to his name turning out to own a musical instrument.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Unqualified' looks like a slight on the sailor's training and is the definition, in the sense of a statement with no qualifications attached rather than a person without papers.
annotation.definitionFit: Absolute means with no qualification or reservation attached — an absolute refusal is an unqualified one.

entries.clue: Volunteers to take tops from boxes (6)

indicatorNotes.take: To take something is to carry it off, so the letter named beside it is lifted out and does not come back.

blocks.note: coffers are strongboxes, the chests a treasury keeps its money in
the letter at the head of COFFERS, which is the one that goes; the plural chimes with the boxes, though a word has only one top

annotation.surface: A helper stepping up to lift the lids off a stack of boxes.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Volunteers' at the front reads as the people rather than the verb, a swap the clue never flags. Coffers is worth banking: it turns up in clues far more often than in life.
annotation.definitionFit: To volunteer help is to offer it, and the tenses match too: he volunteers, he offers.

entries.clue: Comparison is backed by distance (6)

indicatorNotes.backed: Something backed is turned to face the other way, so the short word before it is read from its end.

blocks.note: IS turned round reads SI
a mile is a fixed distance, 1,760 yards

annotation.surface: A comparison that has the weight of the long journey behind it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backed by' reads as one phrase meaning supported, and splitting it is the whole job: 'backed' turns the two letters before it while 'by' merely joins. The comparison wanted is the 'like' or 'as' kind.
annotation.definitionFit: A simile compares one thing to another using like or as — quiet as a mouse — so it is a comparison.

entries.clue: Is furious when article goes into looks (7)

indicatorNotes.goes into: What goes into something ends up inside it, so the short word sits within the longer one.

blocks.note: one who looks sees, and the clue's -s ending carries over
the definite article is THE, and three letters is what the space allows

annotation.surface: Anger at a magazine piece the moment it turns to the subject of people's looks.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Article' is the grammar kind rather than the newspaper kind — a, an or the, with the letter count deciding which. The definition is a whole phrase, 'Is furious', which keeps the final S out of sight.
annotation.definitionFit: To seethe is to boil with anger kept in, so somebody who seethes is furious — matching the clue's third-person 'is'.

entries.clue: Left in despair - like Ebenezer? (7)

annotation.definitionNote: Ebenezer is one example rather than the quality itself, which is what the question mark admits.

indicatorNotes.in: 'In' puts what stands before it inside what stands after, so the single letter lands within the longer word.

blocks.note: misery is despair, wretchedness of spirit
l is the standard abbreviation for left

annotation.surface: Somebody abandoned to their despair, just as a man called Ebenezer was.
annotation.walkthrough: Ebenezer Scrooge is the tight-fisted old man of Dickens's A Christmas Carol, and the first name alone is enough to point at him. 'Left in despair' reads as one sad phrase and is really an instruction with a letter buried in it.
annotation.definitionFit: Ebenezer Scrooge, the hoarding skinflint of A Christmas Carol, is the standard byword for being mean with money.

entries.clue: I'm in the property to make a valuation (8)

indicatorNotes.in: 'In' places what comes before it inside what comes after, so those two letters break the longer word open.

blocks.note: an estate is a property, the house and its land together
the contraction hands over its two letters as written, the apostrophe dropped

annotation.surface: A surveyor ringing in to say they are inside the house and about to value it.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue is one plain sentence a valuer might really say, which is the whole disguise. Contractions like this one are used as letter chunks far more often than solvers expect.
annotation.definitionFit: To estimate a property is to put a figure on what it is worth, which is making a valuation.

entries.clue: Incompetent, in record time (5)

blocks.note: the word is taken over as it stands
an EP is an extended-play record, longer than a single and shorter than an album
t is the standard abbreviation for time

annotation.surface: Managing to bungle something faster than anyone has ever bungled it before.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In record time' is a stock phrase, and that is exactly why it splits so neatly into three pieces. The comma after the definition is the only seam the setter leaves.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody inept is clumsy and unskilled at the task in hand, which is what calling them incompetent says.

entries.clue: Almost submerged by a thin layer (5)

blocks.note: the article is taken over as it stands
the painter's word for watered-down colour brushed thinly over a whole sheet

annotation.surface: Something all but drowned under a film of water.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Thin layer' is the painter's wash — colour spread so thin the paper still shows through. 'Almost' is doing real work in the definition: the answer means water covering a surface, not closing over it.
annotation.definitionFit: A deck awash has water running over it without being under it, which is being almost submerged.

entries.clue: Australian crook is macabre (4)

annotation.definitionNote: 'Australian' is a usage label rather than part of the sense: crook only means unwell in Australian English.

blocks.note: in Australia, crook is how you describe yourself when you are unwell
the taste for death and gruesomeness that a joke can have

annotation.surface: A bent character from Australia with a taste for the gruesome.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crook' reads as a criminal, which is the whole trap — in Australia it is what you call yourself when you are off work. The second half is the modern sense, used of a joke in poor taste.
annotation.definitionFit: Crook is Australian and New Zealand slang for unwell — feeling crook — while a joke called sick is a macabre one.

entries.clue: Sound dissatisfied with drink (4)

indicatorNotes.Sound: Sound asks for the noise a word makes, so what follows is taken by ear rather than by spelling.

blocks.note: somebody dissatisfied whines about it, and spoken aloud that word loses nothing but its H

annotation.surface: Grumbling your way through a glass of something.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sound dissatisfied' reads as a note to an actor, and 'sound' does both jobs at once: it sets up the complaint and it flags the ear. An H is all that separates the two spellings.
annotation.definitionFit: Wine is the drink pressed and fermented from grapes, the plain noun the clue's last word asks for.

entries.clue: One will support the woman in a depression (8)

annotation.definitionNote: The definition is a relative clause with its 'who' left out — one who will support — which is how a noun comes out of a verb phrase.

indicatorNotes.in: 'In' drops what stands before it inside what stands after, so the short word is swallowed by the longer.

blocks.note: a dent is a depression knocked into a surface, and the article in front of it comes along
her is the pronoun standing in for the woman

annotation.surface: A promise to stand by a woman who has sunk into low spirits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Depression' looks like the woman's mood and is really a dent in a surface, with the 'a' in front of it supplying a letter rather than scenery. The support meant is backing a cause, not holding somebody up.
annotation.definitionFit: An adherent is a committed supporter of a party, faith or cause — one who sticks to it and will back it.

entries.clue: Informer isn't disturbing church (6)

indicatorNotes.disturbing: To disturb something is to put it out of its settled arrangement, so those letters will not stay where they are.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, four letters once the apostrophe is dropped
ch is the standard abbreviation for church
anagram indicator

annotation.surface: An assurance that the informer is not the one causing trouble in the parish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Disturbing' sits between the two chunks and could shuffle either side, which is what makes the fodder easy to set wrongly. Apostrophes never count as letters, so isn't offers four.
annotation.definitionFit: A snitch is somebody who tells the authorities what others have done, which is what an informer does.

entries.clue: Pen was first to be fashioned (6)

blocks.note: a sty is the pen a pig is kept in
whoever was first in the race led it

annotation.surface: A writing pen that came before all the others.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pen' is the pig's, not the biro's, and that swap is the whole clue — the surface spends its effort making you picture the other one. 'Was first' is past tense, which is where the last letter comes from.
annotation.definitionFit: Hair or a garment that has been styled has been shaped and fashioned into a particular form.
